chunks: "There are three ways to stop a motor. Coast: switch everything off and let friction slow it.
Short-circuit brake: tie both motor terminals together, so the back-EMF drives current through the winding resistance and the rotor decelerates.
And reverse-voltage braking, or plugging: apply the opposite polarity while it's still spinning.
A half-bridge, with the motor returned to ground, can do the short brake: turn on the low-side FET and both terminals sit at ground.
It can't plug, because it can't apply reverse voltage. An H-bridge can short brake by turning on both low sides, and can also plug by reversing the legs, so it can stop faster.
Numbers make it concrete. Take a 12 volts motor with 1 ohm winding resistance spinning at no-load speed, so the back-EMF is about 12 volts.
Shorting it gives about 12 amps and the current decays with speed.
Plugging gives 12 plus 12 over 1 ohm, so 24 amps, twice the stall current and twice the braking torque at the start.
With my example parameters the plug stop takes about 35 milliseconds while the short brake takes about 115 milliseconds to get down to ten percent.
The cost is stress: higher peak current, more winding heating, a mechanical jolt, brush arcing, and energy pumped from the supply, and if I don't cut the drive at zero speed the motor just reverses."
